content/tasktrackr/phases/01-requirement.title: Requirements
content/tasktrackr/phases/01-requirement.brief:
## Your task

The TaskTrackr backlog is almost complete. Product has signed off on **US-1, US-2, US-3 and US-5** (shown read-only beside your story), but the **overdue report** story was never written, and the team cannot build what nobody has specified.

TaskTrackr is a task manager for people juggling study and work: a Python API over a SQLite database and a React front end in TypeScript, where tasks live in lists, carry a priority and an optional due date, and can be searched, filtered and commented on. This release covers lists and tasks, completing and reopening a task, filtering and searching a list, an overdue report, and a late marker on the rows a person is already looking at. Accounts, sync, notifications and anything that sends a message to a human being are out of scope.

Complete your story, US-4:

1. **Write user story US-4** for the overdue report, in the standard format:
   `As a <persona>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>.`
2. **Add at least two acceptance criteria** in **Given / When / Then** form. Make them *testable* — a machine should be able to verify each one. At least one criterion must settle an edge case: what about a task **due today**? What about a task that is **already completed**?
3. **Say where the report appears.** Dana asked for one place to look, and told you it is not a filter on the list. A requirement can name the surface without designing it.
4. **Add a scope note** — one or two sentences on what the overdue report will **not** do in this release.

To pass the checks, tag one criterion happy path and one boundary (the task due today), and add at least one out-of-scope line.

Interview Dana before you write. She has ten minutes and she has already decided more than you would expect: the boundary, completed tasks, tasks with no due date, the order, what an empty report says, and where she wants to read it. One thing she will not decide is whether the report is a new screen or a new endpoint — that is your problem, and phase 2 is where you answer it.

Later phases build on your story, so the review reads the meaning of your requirements as well as their shape. An epic relationship is optional; if you add one, link it to an epic you have defined.

### Number your criteria the way the rest of the project reads them

Your story's id is **US-4**, and criterion ids are local to it: AC-1, AC-2, and so on. The rest of the project qualifies those same ids as US-4/AC-1, US-4/AC-2, and so on.

Every criterion in this project has an id. US-2/AC-1 is the first criterion of US-2, and the testing phase files each seeded bug against the one criterion that should catch it. Yours are the ones you are about to mint, so write them in this order:

- **US-4/AC-1** — the report itself: a task whose due date has passed appears in it.
- **US-4/AC-2** — the boundary: a task due **today** is not in it yet.
- **US-4/AC-3** — the exclusion: a task you have **completed** is not in it, however late it was.

Two of the eight bugs in phase 4 are filed against AC-2 and AC-3. Number them differently and the mapping still works, but you will be reading someone else's numbering for four phases.

### What good looks like

- The story names a real persona from the provided backlog and a concrete benefit.
- Every criterion could be turned into an automated test without further discussion.
- The reader can tell where the report appears and what a row of it shows.
- No vague words like *fast*, *user-friendly* or *and so on* — nothing testable follows them.

### Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor to critique your draft, propose edge cases you may have missed, or explain what makes a criterion testable. It will not write the story for you — in this phase the requirement decisions are yours, and the next five phases build on what you write here.

When you are ready, press **Submit for review**. Every required criterion and its evidence must pass review before the next phase opens.

content/tasktrackr/phases/02-design.intro:
TaskTrackr runs as two services on one origin. The web service is web/serve.js. It serves the built front end and forwards every /api request to the API, so the browser talks to one origin and there is no CORS. API_URL tells the web service where the API is, and in Deployment it is the line that breaks the deployment.

The API is Flask over SQLite, in three layers with one direction of dependency. The routes are the only code that knows about HTTP: they parse the query string, call the repository and return JSON, with no SQL and no rules. The repository is the only code that knows SQL: filtering, ordering and the overdue rule live there, so they can be tested without a request. One errors module builds every error: an object with a code and a message, sent with a real status code.

The front end mirrors that split: one client module is the only code that fetches, hooks hold the data, lib/overdue.ts holds the one rule the front end owns, and pages and components render. Nothing in the front end filters a list that came back from the API, because a filter has to be right about rows that were never downloaded.

Both halves are written against the shared contracts: the API contract, which the routes publish and the front end mirrors, and the screen contract, which says which screens exist, what each one shows and which operation feeds it. Implementation and Testing hold you to both.

Completing a task shows the path every request takes. The browser posts to /api/tasks/7/complete on its own origin, web/serve.js forwards it to API_URL, the route reads the id and calls the repository, and the repository writes the status and the completion time in one statement and reads the row back. An unknown id becomes task_not_found, sent as a 404. The same path runs in the preview, in development and in Docker Compose; only API_URL changes.

The architecture is settled: two services, the proxy, SQLite, hash routing and the three-layer split on each side. It is not yours to reopen.
content/tasktrackr/phases/02-design.title: Design
content/tasktrackr/phases/02-design.brief:
The architecture is settled, and the Background describes it: two services, a proxy, a SQLite database and three layers on each side. What is not settled is the design of the feature you specified in Requirements, and the contract the next three phases will hold you to.

You work in the Design room's tabs: UML model, API contract, Screens, Sequence diagram, Decisions and Review. Everything you write there is graded together.

In the UML model, complete the data model with every entity and field the stories to design for force. US-3 filters by status and searches the title. US-4 cannot work until the model can say when a task was due. A tag belongs to more than one task and a task carries more than one tag, so say how that is stored. Then add the operations, each naming the story it satisfies: completeTask for US-2, with what it returns and what an unknown id does; listTasks for US-3, with the legal status values, how the keyword matches and the order the rows come back in; and getOverdue for US-4, with the boundary rule your own criteria decided.

In the API contract, fill the four gaps the starting point leaves: the rest of the tasks entity and the tables it needs, the query and the failures of listTasks, the two empty operation rows, and the error catalogue. Every code an operation names is declared in the catalogue with its status and its meaning, and at least one of them is a 404.

In Screens, the overdue report has a row and it is empty. Name the component, the story it satisfies, the operation it reads, the components it renders, and the sentence it shows when nothing is overdue. Dana was clear about that last one in the interview: an empty list with no words looks like a bug.

In the Sequence diagram, trace the overdue request from the browser to the database and back, and name at least one of your operations on it.

In Decisions, record one decision with the alternative it beat and the trade-off you weighed.

What good looks like: every operation carries the id of the story it satisfies, so nothing in the backlog lands nowhere and nothing in the contract serves no one. The contract answers inputs, outputs and failures as sentences, not as empty labels. The screen contract names one operation per screen; a screen that reads no operation shows nothing. The decision reads like something a reviewer could challenge, and you could defend.

Check the design runs the floor before you submit. It asks for at least three entities and two relations; at least three operations, each with an input and a return; every story traced to an operation or an entity that names it; at least three endpoints and an error catalogue in the API contract; at least one screen, each with its component, the operation it reads, the components it renders and an empty-state sentence; a sequence diagram that names an operation; and at least one decision with its rationale and its trade-off.

Ask the AI mentor to compare options, to poke holes in a contract, or to say what a reviewer would want from a decision. It proposes and critiques. The design stays yours.

Maintenance opens its change request against the operations you name here. Implementation inherits these exact operations, and Testing tests them. When you are ready, press Submit for review. Every required criterion and its evidence must pass review before the next phase opens.

content/tasktrackr/phases/03-implementat.title: Implementation
content/tasktrackr/phases/03-implementat.brief:
## Your task

TaskTrackr is built and it runs. The lists, the comments, the schema, the error envelope, the
router, the pages and every route and component around yours are written and locked. What is
missing is the code behind the five sentences your design phase wrote — three in the Python API
and two in the TypeScript front end — and each one is marked `TODO(learner)`.

1. **`list_tasks` in `api/repository/tasks.py`** *(US-3)* — the tasks in one list, narrowed by
   `status`, `q` and `tag`, highest priority first with ties by ascending id. A status the
   contract does not know is a `ValueError`, which the route already turns into a 400.
2. **`overdue_tasks` in `api/repository/tasks.py`** *(US-4)* — open tasks whose due date is
   **strictly before** the day passed in. No due date is never overdue; already done is never
   overdue. Most overdue first, then higher priority, then id.
3. **`complete_task` in `api/routes/tasks.py`** *(US-2)* — mark a task done and answer with it.
   An id nobody has is a 404 carrying the code `task_not_found`.
4. **`isOverdue` in `web/src/lib/overdue.ts`** *(US-4, US-5)* — the same boundary rule, in
   TypeScript, over data the browser already has. `web/src/components/TaskRow.tsx` is locked and
   calls it: write the rule once and a badge appears in a component you did not write.
5. **`useTasks` in `web/src/hooks/useTasks.ts`** *(US-3)* — ask the API for one list's tasks,
   send only the filters that are set, and hand the screen `{ tasks, loading, error, reload }`.
   A request that failed is an error, not an empty list.

`PRIORITY_ORDER`, `TASK_SELECT`, `get_task` and `fail` are already written above and beside the
Python stubs; `daysLate`, `byMostOverdue` and `queryFor` are written above the TypeScript ones.
Use them. The phase is about the five rules, not about SQLite row factories or query strings.

### Workflow

- Press **Run visible tests** any time. Two suites run one after the other and the report groups
  them: `tests/test_tasks_api.py`, four cases through Flask's own test client, and
  `web/src/lib/overdue.test.ts`, two cases on the boundary. All six fail right now, because the
  stubs raise `NotImplementedError` and throw `Error`.
- Press **Run app** to start your own API and your own front end and use them in the Preview
  tab. The database is seeded, so there is something to look at. Before you start, the lists
  page works and a list's tasks do not — that is the gap you are about to fill.
- The fixtures the API suite uses — `client`, `make_list`, `make_task` — are in
  `tests/conftest.py`, which is locked but open to read. They drive the API through Flask's test
  client, so a test reads exactly like the request it stands for.
- **Submit PR-3** runs both visible suites, two **hidden suites** of fourteen and eight
  cases over the same five contracts, and static analysis (leftover TODOs, banned constructs,
  complexity).
- Run before you submit. The rubric's process criterion notices.

### What good looks like

- Each gap is a few lines that lean on what the module already offers. `list_tasks` collects the
  conditions it was actually given; `overdue_tasks` is one SELECT with three conditions;
  `complete_task` is the same three lines as the four routes around it; `isOverdue` is three
  comparisons; `useTasks` is state, an effect and an answer for the failure.
- Every sentence of the docstring is true, not only the six assertions you can see. The hidden
  suites ask about an unknown id, a keyword in the middle of a title, two filters at once, a task
  due today, a task that was late but is finished, a badge on a row, a filter that should not
  have been sent, and a request that failed.
- The two overdue rules agree. You are writing the same boundary twice, once in SQL and once in
  TypeScript, and the day they disagree is the day a task is late in the report and on time on
  the row. The testing phase will ask you to prove it in both languages.
- The contract in `shared/contract/api.json` is the same one you completed in design. When your
  code and that file disagree, one of them is wrong and it is worth knowing which.

### Using the AI mentor well

Ask it to read a traceback with you, to point you at the SQL, the Flask construct or the React
hook the codebase already uses, or to talk through a boundary case. It will not write a function
body, and pasting a finished answer from anywhere defeats the phase — the hidden suites are only
interesting if the code is yours.

When you are ready, press **Submit PR-3**. Every required criterion and its evidence must pass review before the next phase opens.

### Your accepted screen copy

The read-only overdue page uses the title and empty-state sentence from the retained Design submission that passed when Implementation opened. Its source submission is recorded in `shared/contract/accepted-screen-copy.json`; the read-only screen contract shows the same text. Later draft edits do not change this accepted handoff. Older work without a retained accepted source uses an explicitly labelled reference copy.

content/tasktrackr/phases/04-testing.intro: Write the acceptance suites that prove US-2, US-3, US-4 and US-5 on both sides of the contract, and catch the bugs we planted in the API and in the front end.
content/tasktrackr/phases/04-testing.title: Testing
content/tasktrackr/phases/04-testing.brief:
## Your task

Your implementation passed, but "the code runs" is not the same as "the behaviour is proven". In this phase you write the acceptance suites for TaskTrackr — the suites a team would run before every release.

The application has two halves and so does the phase. The whole application is mounted in the workspace and locked, so the two test files you open are the only things that change.

- **`tests/test_acceptance.py`** tests the **API's HTTP routes** through Flask's in-process test client.
- **`web/src/acceptance.test.tsx`** tests the **front end** in the supplied jsdom DOM harness.

### The API half, in `tests/test_acceptance.py`

1. **US-2, completing a task.** Completion is stored, not merely answered, and an id no task has is refused with the status code and the error code `shared/contract/api.json` names.
2. **US-3, listing, filtering and ordering.** Status filtering, keyword matching that ignores case, and the ordering promise: high before medium before low, ties by id.
3. **US-4, the overdue report.** Open tasks with a due date strictly before the day you ask about. Cover the boundary — **due today is not overdue** — and keep out a task that has no due date and a task that was finished late.

What is already in the file:

- **`client`** is Flask's test client, wired to a fresh in-memory database for every test. `client.post("/api/tasks/3/complete")` is the request a browser would make, minus the socket, and it goes through the same routing, status codes and JSON your front end will meet.
- **`make_list`** and **`make_task`** build a starting state through the API, and the `add` and `day` helpers at the top of the file save you the repetition.
- **`today()`** reads the run clock. See below.

### The front-end half, in `web/src/acceptance.test.tsx`

4. **US-5, the late marker on a row.** A row for a task whose due date has gone by carries a marker saying how many whole days late it is. A finished task carries none, however late it was. A task with no due date carries none either.
5. **US-3 again, from the other side.** The search box has to survive the next filter: when a status is chosen as well, the request the front end sends still carries the keyword.

What is already in that file:

- **`render`** puts a component in jsdom and **`screen`** asks questions of that DOM. This harness checks rendered content and interactions without opening a browser or proving its visual layout. `screen.getByTestId(...)` throws when nothing matches; `screen.queryByTestId(...)` answers `null`, which is what you want when the point of the test is that something is absent.
- **`renderHook`** runs a hook on its own, and **`waitFor`** waits for the state it settles into.
- **`assert`** is node's assert module. There is no `expect` and no matcher library here.
- **`aTask(...)`** and **`answerWith(...)`** are in `web/src/testing/fixtures.ts`, locked and worth reading once. `aTask` gives you a task with the contract's defaults so a test names only the fact it is about; `answerWith` answers every request with one canned response and collects the URLs that were asked for. There is no server behind these tests, and a test that reaches for the network is told so.
- **`today()`** and **`daysAgo(n)`** are the twins of `tests/clock.py`, and they read the same run clock.

The testids the application already carries, so you can ask for exactly the thing you mean:

| testid | what it is |
|---|---|
| `task-row` | one row |
| `task-title`, `task-priority`, `task-due`, `task-tag` | what the row says |
| `overdue-badge` | the late marker, and its wording is "3 days late" |
| `complete-task`, `reopen-task` | the button the row offers |
| `filter-status`, `filter-q`, `filter-tag` | the filter bar |

### How you are graded

- **Pass on a healthy application** — a test that fails on correct code is a bug in the test.
- **Mutation testing** — on submit, your suites also run against **eight secretly broken copies of the application**: six of the API and two of the front end. A strong suite fails on every one of them, which is what "killing a mutant" means. Weak assertions let them through.
- **Coverage mapping** — completing, filtering, the overdue report and the late marker each need at least one test, and **six tests across the two files** is the floor.

Press **Run my tests** while you work: both suites run one after the other and the report groups them under **API tests** and **Front end**. The broken copies only run on submit. Open **Execution evidence** to inspect each case, its failure details and the run's console output. These suites do not replace a separate browser check of the running application.

Name each test after the criterion it proves and keep the ids from the requirements phase — `US-3/AC-2`, `US-5/AC-2`. Every planted bug is filed against one criterion, so a surviving copy names the criterion your suite has not proved yet.

### The response, or the next request

One habit is worth more than any other on the API side. A handler can answer `"status": "done"` and write nothing at all, and the only thing that can tell you is asking for the task again:

```python
client.post(f"/api/tasks/{task['id']}/complete")
again = client.get(f"/api/tasks/{task['id']}").get_json()
assert again["status"] == "done"
```

A suite that stops at the first response passes on an API that forgets everything.

The front-end habit is the twin of it: assert the URL the screen asked for, not only that something came back. A hook that quietly drops a parameter still renders whatever the server sent, and only the URL can tell you.

```tsx
const urls = answerWith({ body: [] });
// ... run the hook, wait for it to settle ...
assert.ok(urls[0].includes('q=rent'), urls[0]);
```

### The run clock

Both your suites have a boundary in them — due today is not overdue — and a boundary about dates is only testable if you decide what day it is. Read the day through `tests/clock.py` on the API side:

```python
from tests.clock import today

def day(offset):
    return (today() + timedelta(days=offset)).isoformat()
```

and through `web/src/testing/clock.ts` on the front end, where `daysAgo(3)` is the date three days ago. Build every due date from them. Then pin the clock in the **Run clock** control beside the criteria: with a date pinned, your suites, the reference runs and all eight broken copies see that same day, so the kill matrix means the same thing tomorrow as it does now. With nothing pinned they all see the machine's date.

A test that names a fixed date rots. A test that reads the machine's clock is a different test every day. Reading the clock through one function is how a real suite stays honest. Changing the clock costs you no attempt and invalidates no verdict — it is a parameter of the next run, not an event.

### What good looks like

- One behaviour per test, named after the criterion it proves.
- Assertions on stored state, on exact ordering, and on what the screen actually shows — not on "it did not raise".
- Both sides of every boundary, every error path checked by status code **and** error code, and the absent case asserted as carefully as the present one.

### Using the AI mentor well

Ask about boundary values, what makes an assertion strong, how to tell a response apart from stored state, or how to ask a rendered row a question. It will not reveal the planted bugs — working out what could break is the skill being trained.

When you are ready, press **Submit PR-4**. Every required criterion and its evidence must pass review before the next phase opens.

content/tasktrackr/phases/05-deployment.title: Deployment
content/tasktrackr/phases/05-deployment.brief:
TaskTrackr is implemented and tested. Now make it shippable. It ships as two services: a Python API and a Node process that serves the front end and forwards /api to the API. Three configuration files are scaffolded and incomplete, and the runbook is yours to write in the Runbook tab.

In api/Dockerfile the base image, the environment and the volume are set. Replace the three TODO(learner) markers: set a WORKDIR for the app; COPY what the image needs (requirements.txt for the pip install below it, api/ and ops/ to run at all, and docker-compose.yml, because ops/selfcheck.py reads the deployment this image belongs to); and define an ENTRYPOINT in exec form, so that docker run tasktrackr --selfcheck reaches api/main.py. web/Dockerfile beside it is finished and locked. It is the worked example: two stages, the build tools left behind in the first. Read it when a line will not come.

In docker-compose.yml both services, one network and one named volume are wired. Replace the two TODO(learner) markers: give api a healthcheck the web service can wait on (web already declares condition: service_healthy, and the api image carries python3 and nothing else, no curl and no wget), and point API_URL at the api service. Inside a compose network a service is reachable by its own name on a port it exposes; localhost inside a container means that container.

In .github/workflows/ci.yml there are three jobs, because this application has two suites and two images. Checkout, the runtime and the install are wired in each of them; what is missing is the line that runs something. In test, add a step that runs the API suite, which package.json calls test:api. In web, add a step that runs the front-end suite, test:web. In build, add a step that builds both images: one build per Dockerfile, each with -f because both are built from the project root, or one compose build for the pair. That job already needs both suites, so a red test never reaches it.

The Runbook tab holds the runbook an operator reads at 3am, in five sections. Environment: each setting's name, what it controls and its default; TASKTRACKR_DB and API_URL are the two an operator changes, and PORT and HOST are worth an entry each. Health checks: a command that proves the deployment is alive and the output that proves it; the check compose itself waits on and the selfcheck that reads the whole deployment are both good answers. Rollback: the steps that get the previous known-good images back, in order, and what a rollback does not undo. Data: where the database lives, which commands keep it and which delete it, and how to take a backup and put one back. Incident: written for you from the drill page when you close INCIDENT-1. Check the runbook lists what the floor still asks for.

Deploying is the worked example of an operator's line: docker compose up -d --build builds both images, starts api, waits for it to report healthy, then starts web on port 5173. Nothing else is needed on the host.

Press Run selfcheck to check the saved configuration. The isolated runner compiles the Python source, reads the launcher from your api/Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT or CMD and WORKDIR, and invokes it with the project's --selfcheck argument. ops/selfcheck.py imports the Flask application, initializes the SQLite schema, checks that the Compose file gives web an API_URL naming a declared service and port, and reports whether a web bundle exists. Its success line reads selfcheck: web reaches api, 13 routes, 5 tables, and there web reaches api means the declared Compose address is consistent: no network request is made. This local check does not build either Docker image, install the Dockerfile's dependencies, execute GitHub Actions, start Compose services, or prove live HTTP health. A real release also needs successful image builds, live service checks and a versioned release record; do not claim those from this selfcheck.

The drill page carries INCIDENT-1. Start it once your selfcheck passes: it runs the same isolated check against a faulted copy of your compose file and records the output. The symptom on the day was the whole application loading with every page empty, while the API was healthy and its logs were quiet. Read the output and name the setting at fault, check your own docker-compose.yml for the same mistake, run the health check against your own files, then close the incident on the drill page with the root cause naming the setting, the fix you made, and one action item. The review reads the incident.

What good looks like: every runbook entry carries a real command or sentence, not a name alone; both suites run in CI, so a red test in either language fails the pipeline, and the job that builds the images waits on both of them; and the incident names the setting, API_URL, and the line that changed, not just that the site was broken.

content/tasktrackr/phases/06-maintenance.intro: A change request arrives on a system that already works. Ship it without breaking anything.
content/tasktrackr/phases/06-maintenance.title: Maintenance
content/tasktrackr/phases/06-maintenance.brief:
TaskTrackr shipped, people use it, and one request keeps coming back: change request CR-2, comments on a task. The ticket in the Request tab says what it asks for and how the change will be accepted.

The codebase is the finished one. Lists, tasks, tags, filters and the overdue report all work, and the front end reads them. Your job is to add the new capability without breaking any of it.

In api/repository/comments.py, implement add_comment(conn, task_id, author, body) and list_comments(conn, task_id). add_comment stores one comment and returns it in the shape the contract publishes: id, task_id, author, body and created_at. An unknown task raises KeyError, in either function. An empty author or an empty body raises ValueError, and whitespace alone is empty. list_comments returns the comments newest first.

In api/routes/comments.py the blueprint is registered and the two handlers are yours. GET /api/tasks/{id}/comments answers 200 with the comments, or 404 task_not_found. POST /api/tasks/{id}/comments answers 201 with the comment, or 400 invalid_comment, or 404 task_not_found. api/routes/tasks.py is the worked example: it turns KeyError into a 404 and ValueError into a 400, and builds both with fail(), so every error this API sends has one shape.

The task row has to show how many comments a task carries, so every task the API returns needs a comment_count. That lives in TASK_SELECT in api/repository/tasks.py, and that one query is read by get_task, list_tasks and overdue_tasks, each of which adds its own WHERE and ORDER BY. So the count has to come back as one value per task, without changing how many rows the query returns; tag_names, a few lines below, already does exactly that against another table. A join in the FROM clause is the obvious move and the wrong one. LIST_SELECT, which computes each list's task_count and open_count, is separate and does not change. The regression suite tells you, and you can run it yourself.

In web/src/components/TaskRow.tsx a task that carries comments wears a badge, 1 comment or 4 comments, and a task with none wears nothing. The badge is a span with className badge badge-comments and data-testid comment-count, in the task-main block beside the overdue badge, which is the same shape a few lines above.

Two contracts travel with the change. shared/contract/api.json is the published HTTP contract: add listComments and addComment in the shape of their neighbours, and the error code addComment answers with. design/contracts.json holds the operations you promised in the design phase, seeded when this phase unlocked: add the two comment operations, their inputs, what they return and the error cases. The conformance ledger holds your code against it.

What 2.0.0 shipped: lists, tasks and tags over a SQLite database with foreign keys enforced; eleven HTTP operations under /api, published in the API contract; three screens behind a hash router; the overdue report, open tasks strictly past their due date, most overdue first, with the day a parameter; two containers and a compose file with a healthcheck and a named volume; the selfcheck; and a seed script. The web service proxies /api, so the application needs no CORS. The comments table is already in api/schema.sql, created by api/db.py, and nothing reads or writes it yet.

Record the change in the change request as you go: in the Request tab, the operations, screens and files it touches; in the Contract tab, the two operations as contract amendments; in the Checks tab, the tests and the acceptance items each covers; in the Release tab, the 2.1.0 release, its summary, the change lines with the acceptance items each covers, and how to roll it back, written for the person who upgrades. Say truthfully whether a schema change is needed.

On submit, a sealed suite runs your new behaviour and a regression suite over everything the earlier phases shipped, across both layers, pooled: a change that costs a regression scores less than no change at all. The visible tests are tests/test_comments_api.py, a three-question smoke of the change, tests/test_lists_api.py and tests/test_tasks_api.py, the regression suite, and web/src/components/TaskRow.test.tsx. Static analysis checks that no TODO markers are left and that complexity stays low. Keep the change small and local.

What good looks like: the new functions read like their neighbours, with the same lookup helper for the unknown-task case, the same _to_comment on the way out, and no second copy of a check that already exists; the regression suite is green before you ever press Submit PR-6; and nothing outside the files the request names has changed.

Ask the mentor how to scope a change safely, what a count in a composed query has to look like, or why regression tests belong in a maintenance change; it will not write the SQL, the routes or the badge for you. Press Run regression tests as you work, and Run app to see the count on a real row. When you are ready, press Submit PR-6. This is the final phase, so passing completes the project.

- One decision in the decision log, the alternative you rejected and the
  reason it lost.

check your design against that list yourself.

apps/api/test/fixtures/upload-packs/star.brief:
# Testing: prove the backlog

Write acceptance tests for SH-1 to SH-4 in `tests/test_acceptance.py` (the API)
and `web/src/lib/acceptance.test.ts` (the page). The graders run your suites
against the working application and against copies of it with bugs planted in
them; a good suite passes on the first and fails on every one of the others.

## What good looks like

- Every test passes against the working application.
- At least one test per acceptance criterion, asserting what a person or a
  client would see, not only a status code.
- Cases about the author filter, lending, returning and the "on loan" line.

## Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor which acceptance criterion a test of yours does not yet cover.

The incident is closed on the drill page with what the drill broke, the fix and one action item.

Using the AI mentor well: ask what each Dockerfile instruction changes about the image, and write the instructions yourself.

apps/api/test/fixtures/upload-packs/star.brief:
Change request CHG-1. The library has asked for the shelf to follow the order a librarian shelves in: by the author's surname, then by title, then by id. Change both layers (api/shelf.py and web/src/lib/shelf.ts) without breaking anything the shelf already did.

What good looks like: the API and the page agree on the new order. Lending, returning and the author filter behave exactly as before. The visible regression cases pass before you submit.

Record the change in the change request as you go: in the Request tab, what the change touches; in the Checks tab, the tests and the acceptance items each covers; in the Release tab, the release, its change lines and how to roll it back.

Using the AI mentor well: ask the mentor which existing behaviour your change could break, then run the regression cases to find out.
